source.title: Brain-model neural similarity reveals abstractive summarization performance
source.authors: Zhe-Jun Zhang; Shaoting Guo; Wenqing Zhou; Yin-zhuo Luo; Ying-Qi Zhu; Lin Zhang; Lei Li

record.tranche_reason: The study reports exploratory representational-similarity comparisons between layers of different models, a different measurement setting from the scale-and-capability claim. It does not test whether alignment rises with model scale or capability.
record.gate_note: The main RSA analyses compare language-model representations with human EEG representations, and the layer interventions measure summarization performance; neither measures convergence between models as defined by the claim versions. The exploratory cross-model layer comparisons in Supplementary Fig. S1 are included because the text reports their similarity trends. The study's random-initialization controls concern model-to-brain RSA and are not rows for the claim.
record.test_reason: The main results are brain–model RSA and layer-ablation correlations, which do not measure convergence between models. The only model-to-model result is an exploratory, qualitative inter-layer RSA heatmap across three fine-tuned encoder-decoder models (Supp. Fig. S1). It has no scale or capability variation (V1, V2), no seeds (V3), no mapping or stitching (V4), no features (V5), no alternative metrics or inputs (V6), and no completeness or cause test (V7). The Platonic Representation Hypothesis is invoked only as an interpretation.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly wrong in emphasis. The authors' main conclusion is that encoder layers more similar to human EEG representations matter more for summarization: manipulating them causes larger ROUGE drops, which holds after controlling for perplexity. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis appears only as a side interpretation of the exploratory cross-model heatmaps and brain-similarity results. They suggest the shared Transformer architecture may explain the cross-model similarities.
record.recipe_differences: Exploratory RSA comparisons among encoder layers of three fine-tuned summarization models; no scale sweep or performance-linked cross-model alignment test.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported cross-model RSA trend differs across model pairs and layer depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Exploratory inter-layer RSA between the encoders of BART-large, PEGASUS-large and T5-large (fine-tuned on different summarization data) shows 'extensive regions of similarity'. PEGASUS–T5 similarity is higher than either model's similarity with BART. The depth trend differs by pair: BART–PEGASUS rises then falls, BART–T5 rises, PEGASUS–T5 falls. No numeric values are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-model representational similarity among fixed-scale fine-tuned language models exists, but its profile across layer depth depends on the model pair.

fits_no_version.finding: RSA between model encoder layers and human EEG increases significantly with layer depth for BART, PEGASUS and T5 (Jonckheere–Terpstra test, e.g. T5 Full window Z=7.578). Randomly initialized controls show no such increase. RSA values are on the order of 0.02–0.04.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Brain–model representational alignment increases with layer depth in trained models (brain alignment, not model–model convergence).

record.problems: The cross-model comparison is exploratory and reported only as qualitative trends; numerical RSA values and uncertainty estimates for these pairwise trends are not stated. The study does not vary model scale or directly assess capability.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant rows left out. Brain-to-model RSA results and layer-manipulation performance results were excluded because they do not measure the model-to-model convergence specified by the claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no variation in model size or capability; only three models of similar (large) scale are compared.
All: no vision models or paired image–caption data.
All: no models of the same architecture trained from different seeds.
All: no mapping, stitching or relative-representation transfer between models.
All: no feature- or circuit-level comparison.
All: only cosine RSMs with Spearman RSA on one set of 1459 tokens; no alternative metric or input distribution.
All: no quantification of how complete cross-model alignment is and no plateau test. The shared Transformer architecture is offered only as a speculative cause, untested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 relation and its V7 limits_scope label are removed. The cross-model analysis is qualitative, appears only in a supplementary figure, and measures layer-depth profiles, not convergence with scale or the completeness or causes of alignment. The three models differ in architecture variant, objective and fine-tuning data, but none of these factors is varied systematically.

versions.untested_parts: Whether alignment between independently trained models rises with model size or capability.
Cross-modal alignment between vision and language models on paired images and captions as model performance improves.
Convergence across random seeds of the same architecture and shared features or subspaces.
Mapping representations between models, stitching layers, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
Recurrence of shared interpretable features or circuits across models.
Whether model-to-model convergence changes under other similarity measures, settings, or input distributions.

Whether alignment is far from complete or plateaus, and whether shared data or objectives rather than a common model of reality explain it; the study provides no numerical completeness assessment or test of those proposed causes.

rows.value: Similarity initially increased with depth, then decreased in deeper layers.
rows.locator: Exploratory RSA analysis; Supplementary Fig. S1
rows.note: The text describes the trend but gives no numerical RSA values for this comparison.
rows.check: The layer-depth trend of cross-model RSA (BART–PEGASUS rises, then falls) does not measure what V7 names: completeness, plateau with scale, or shared data or objectives as the cause. It is qualitative only, from a supplementary heatmap, with no numbers or baseline.
